common_name: Mrs. Burns' Lemon Basil (New Mexico Heirloom Lemon Basil)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mrs. Burns' Lemon is a New Mexico heirloom lemon basil selected for unusually intense lemon fragrance and strong vigor in heat.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Mrs. Burns' Lemon is a New Mexico heirloom lemon basil long saved and passed along by seed keepers for its unusually intense, true lemon fragrance and flavor, stronger and cleaner than many other lemon basil selections, on plants that grow taller and more vigorously than typical lemon basils even through Gulf South summer heat. The bright citrus flavor makes it outstanding in teas, fish and seafood dishes, fruit salads, and infused vinegars or oils. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and keep the plant bushy and productive, and harvest leaves often since frequent picking encourages fuller, more branched growth through the season.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Amethyst is an All-America Selections winner bred for uniform, deep purple color and improved bolt resistance on a compact plant.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun for the deepest, most uniform purple leaf color. Amethyst is an All-America Selections winner bred for consistent, richly saturated purple foliage from seedling stage onward, along with improved resistance to premature bolting compared with older purple basil types, keeping the compact plant productive and attractive for a longer stretch of the growing season. Its uniform color and tidy habit make it useful as an ornamental edible in containers and border plantings as well as a culinary and vinegar-infusing basil. Pinch growing tips regularly to delay flowering and encourage bushier growth, and harvest leaves often to keep new growth coming.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Boxwood basil forms a dense, rounded, globe-shaped mound reminiscent of a small clipped boxwood shrub, useful as an edible edging or container plant.

directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Boxwood basil forms an unusually dense, tightly rounded mound of small, aromatic leaves that closely mimics the look of a miniature clipped boxwood shrub, making it a favorite for formal-looking edible edging, knot gardens, and containers where a tidy, structural basil is wanted alongside its classic sweet basil flavor. Its slow-to-bolt, compact habit needs little shaping beyond occasional light trimming to keep the globe form neat, and regular harvesting for the kitchen doubles as maintenance pruning. Keep soil evenly moist and pick leaves regularly through the season to encourage continued dense, bushy growth.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Extrakta was bred for an unusually high essential oil content, giving it a more concentrated, robust oregano flavor than typical culinary oregano.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; oregano flavor intensity is strongest when grown a bit lean rather than heavily fertilized. Extrakta was selected for an unusually high concentration of essential oils in its leaves, giving a bolder, more pungent, more robustly flavored oregano than many ordinary culinary strains, prized by cooks who want maximum flavor impact from a smaller amount of fresh or dried herb. The compact, mounding perennial forms a tidy clump well suited to an herb garden border or container. Harvest leaves and stems regularly through the growing season, and for the most concentrated flavor for drying, cut just before the plant flowers, when essential oil content peaks.

common_name: Compactum Thyme (Dense Non-Flowering Culinary Edging Thyme)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; Compactum forms a dense, low, mostly non-flowering mound of culinary thyme well suited to edging beds and paths.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; thyme performs poorly and can rot in heavy, wet, or overly rich soil. Compactum is a dense, mounding form of common culinary thyme that stays low and tidy without the sprawling, woody growth typical of standard thyme, and flowers only sparingly, keeping its energy focused on producing tender, flavorful leaves rather than seed. Its neat habit makes it a popular choice for edging garden beds and paths, filling gaps between stepping stones, or growing in containers. Trim lightly after any bloom and shear back by about a third in early spring to keep the mound dense and prevent the center from opening up and becoming woody over time.

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Goodwin Creek is widely regarded as one of the best-performing lavenders for hot, humid Southern climates, tolerating conditions that cause classic English lavenders to rot and decline.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, ideally on a raised bed, berm, or slope to keep roots from sitting in wet soil, especially through humid Gulf South summers. Goodwin Creek Lavender is a hybrid (Lavandula x ginginsii) prized as one of the most reliable lavenders for hot, humid climates where classic English lavender types typically struggle with root and crown rot; it bears silvery, deeply toothed foliage and long-blooming purple-blue flower spikes over an extended season. It tolerates heat and humidity noticeably better than most lavender types, though it is somewhat less cold-hardy, so mulch lightly and avoid heavy winter wet in colder zones within its range. Prune after flowering to maintain a compact, woody shape and avoid the leggy, splayed-open form lavender develops if left unpruned for several years.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Herb Gardening
